summary: Discusses aggregating Diffserv service classes inside high-capacity network cores, where some segments may offer only one forwarding treatment for several classes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5127 explains how a network with few forwarding treatments can still carry traffic that needs different levels of care. It defines what a treatment aggregate is, lists the rules an aggregation must follow, and shows how the service classes from RFC 4594 can be grouped into four aggregates.

subtitle: How to serve several Differentiated Services classes from one forwarding treatment in a backbone.

tldr.problem: A backbone router may have fewer kinds of forwarding treatment than the number of Differentiated Services classes its traffic needs, so several classes have to share one treatment.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a treatment aggregate as a set of service classes served by one forwarding treatment, gives five requirements the aggregation must meet, and maps every class from RFC 4594 into four example aggregates.
tldr.outcome: The four aggregates are an example, not a fixed set. A domain may support more or fewer, and the choice belongs to the network operator.

today: RFC 5127 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It offers guidelines rather than requirements, and it builds on the service classes defined in RFC 4594.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In the core of a high-capacity network, the network is often engineered so that a failed link or router leaves a routed network that still meets the ambient service level agreements. That means there is enough capacity on each link to carry every sold SLA at its maximum rate at the same time, even after re-routing, whether by IP re-routing or by Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) protection-mode switching.

Over-provisioning usually removes the need for quality of service treatment, and in a backbone that is generally true. But as convergence takes longer and access networks get faster, some services still have problems. Delay, jitter and occasional loss are acceptable for elastic applications, while sub-second surges affect real-time applications. Denial of service loads, worms and network disruptions affect routing itself. The objective is to prevent disruption to routing, to protect real-time traffic sensitive to jitter, and to keep loss and delay low for sensitive elastic traffic.

RFC 4594 defines a set of basic Diffserv classes from the point of view of the application needing specific end-to-end behaviour. The classes differ by the application's tolerance of packet loss, delay and delay variation. At some segments of an end-to-end path there are fewer levels of treatment than there are classes to support, so several classes must share one treatment. This document gives guidelines for that aggregation.
sections.plainLanguage: A backbone is usually built with enough spare capacity that every service works without special handling. When that is not true, a router can offer fewer kinds of treatment than the traffic needs, and several classes of traffic must share one. This document explains how to do that safely.

sections.title: Requirements for Aggregation
sections.content:
The document defines a treatment aggregate as the aggregate of Diffserv service classes. It concerns only the forwarding treatment of the aggregated traffic, which may carry several DSCP values. That differs from a behavior aggregate or a traffic aggregate, each of which has a single Diffserv codepoint and a single per hop behavior.

Aggregation has to meet five requirements. The end-to-end network performance characteristic required by the application MUST be supported, expressed by the use of Diffserv service classes. The treatment aggregate MUST meet the strictest requirements of its member service classes. It SHOULD only contain member classes with similar traffic characteristics and performance requirements. The notion of the individual end-to-end service classes MUST NOT be destroyed when aggregation is performed: each domain on the path may aggregate differently, based on the original end-to-end classes. The recommended way to keep that notion is to leave the DSCP marking alone and let classifiers that read the DSCP field direct packets into the right queue, without remarking them. Where a domain insists on its own marking, the original end-to-end class indication must be restored on the way out, possibly with tunnels. Finally, because each treatment aggregate has limited resources, traffic conditioning and admission control SHOULD be performed for each service class that is aggregated into it, with additional control possible on the sum.

Two suggestions sit alongside the requirements. The aggregate and its resources may take historical traffic patterns into account, since a point-to-point service such as a pseudowire has a far more predictable pattern than a multipoint service such as VPLS. Controls other than Diffserv are also available to influence the traffic level offered to an aggregate, including routing metric adjustment and MPLS-based traffic engineering.
sections.plainLanguage: When classes are merged, the merged group must be treated at least as well as the strictest member class needs, and the original marking must survive so that other domains still know what each packet needs. Each class should still be admitted and policed on its own, because the group has a limited amount of resources.

sections.title: Mapping Service Classes into Four Aggregates
sections.content:
The example mapping uses four treatment aggregates and assumes each one has enough resources to honour the behaviour required of every class placed in it. The application performance requirements, namely tolerance of loss, delay and jitter, decide the grouping. The treatment aggregate column of Figure 1 shows that Network Control keeps a low tolerance of loss and delay but tolerates jitter, Real-Time has a very low tolerance of all three, Assured Elastic has a low tolerance of loss and a low to medium tolerance of delay, and Elastic specifies no tolerance at all.

Figure 2 gives the forwarding behaviour to use for each aggregate and the DSCP values to classify into it. Network Control uses the Class Selector behaviour of RFC 2474 and takes CS6. Real-Time uses the Expedited Forwarding behaviour of RFC 3246 and takes EF, CS5, AF41, AF42, AF43, CS4 and CS3. Assured Elastic uses the Assured Forwarding behaviour of RFC 2597 and takes CS2, AF31, AF21, AF11, AF32, AF22, AF12, AF33, AF23 and AF13. Elastic uses the Default behaviour of RFC 2474 and takes Default (CS0) and CS1.

The mapping is a recommendation, not a mandate. A domain need not support every class listed for an aggregate, only the ones it supports itself, and its treatment of the others follows local policy. A domain may also choose a different number of aggregates, for example three, with network control traffic mapped into the Assured Elastic aggregate.
sections.plainLanguage: The four example groups are Network Control for the traffic a network needs to survive a flood, Real-Time for traffic that cannot wait, Assured Elastic for traffic with a promised rate, and Elastic for everything else. Each group keeps the original DSCP marking of its classes and only changes the queue the packets go into.

sections.title: Inside the Four Treatment Aggregates
sections.content:
The Network Control Treatment Aggregate holds the classes that are functionally necessary for the network to survive a denial of service attack or another high-load period, on the theory that the network must protect itself. Its traffic should sit in a common queue with the Class Selector per hop behaviour of RFC 2474, with a lower probability of loss and a relatively deep target mean queue depth, using the min-threshold if RED is in use. This aggregate is for the customer's network control traffic; a provider may treat its own control traffic differently, in a separate class.

The Real-Time Treatment Aggregate holds the real-time, inelastic classes: Telephony, Signaling, Multimedia Conferencing, Real-time Interactive and Broadcast Video. The premise is that real-time traffic is admitted and controlled by an SLA managed at the edge before aggregation, so the level entering the queue is predictable and enforceable, and the queue needs protection from bursts of elastic traffic. Each service class should be conditioned before aggregation, with per-class admission control followed by per-class policing, and further admission control and policing may apply to the sum. The traffic should sit in a common queue with the Expedited Forwarding per hop behaviour of RFC 3246 and RFC 3247.

The Assured Elastic Treatment Aggregate holds elastic traffic using the Assured Forwarding model, where a negotiated SLA carries a committed rate, the ability to exceed it, and possibly a second excess rate, in exchange for a higher chance of loss marked by active queue management or explicit congestion notification. It may include Multimedia Streaming, Low Latency Data, OAM and High-Throughput Data. The AF group and class selector markings of the original classes must be preserved, so AF3x packets stay AF3x marked, and the class selector DSCP must not change. The service should be engineered so that AFn1 and CS2 flows have enough bandwidth for high assurance of delivery. Active queue management should mainly reduce the forwarding rate to the minimum assured rate at congestion points, and the loss probability of AFn1 and CS2 traffic must not exceed that of AFn2, which must not exceed that of AFn3. With RED, the min-threshold sets a target queue depth for each of AFn1 plus CS2, AFn2 and AFn3, and the max-threshold sets the depth above which traffic with that DSCP is dropped or marked.

The Elastic Treatment Aggregate holds the remaining elastic traffic: Standard and Low-Priority Data. There is no intrinsic SLA differentiation, but active queue management or explicit congestion notification still applies. Its traffic should sit in a common queue with the Default per hop behaviour of RFC 2474. The queue management thresholds may be set separately so that Low-Priority Data is dropped before Standard traffic, though that is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of the four groups has its own queue and its own forwarding rule. Network control traffic is kept safe during a flood. Real-time traffic is limited at the edge so the queue never becomes unpredictable. Assured elastic traffic keeps the marks that show its committed and excess rates, and the queue is drained in the right order. Elastic traffic has no promise attached to it at all.

sections.title: Inter-Provider Relationships and the MPLS Example
sections.content:
When treatment aggregates are used at a provider boundary, the document recommends that the inter-provider relationship be based on Diffserv service classes, so that the admission control of each provider domain can follow from the admission control of the supported classes. If the relationship has to be based on the treatment aggregates themselves, the exact content and representation must be agreed between the peering providers.

The appendix works through an example that carries the treatment aggregates over MPLS using an E-LSP, an EXP Inferred PHB Scheduling Class label switched path as defined in RFC 3270. The MPLS EXP field values recommended for the aggregates are 110 for Network Control, 100 for Real-Time, 010 and 011 for Assured Elastic, and 000 and 001 for Elastic. The two values used for Assured Elastic and for Elastic encode two levels of drop precedence, with 010 encoded traffic less likely to be dropped than 011, and 000 less likely than 001. Packets in an LSP with EXP 011 or 001 have a higher probability of being dropped than those with 010 or 000, so with this mapping CS1 marked traffic may be starved during congestion. If a domain supports only one drop precedence for the aggregate, the document recommends 010 for Assured Elastic and 000 for Elastic. Because each domain controls its own EXP use, a domain may allocate the field differently. L-LSP, which supports a single scheduling class per LSP, supports each aggregate per LSP, and the document leaves that mapping to each MPLS domain administration.
sections.plainLanguage: At a boundary between providers, the contract is easier to write in terms of the original service classes than in terms of the four groups. Where the groups themselves are used across a boundary, the appendix shows how to carry them in an MPLS label switched path, using three bits of the EXP field to mark the group and a second value to show which traffic is dropped first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document discusses the policy of using Differentiated Services and its service classes. If it is implemented as described, the network does nothing it was not already allowed to do, so no new security issues should arise from the policy. Because the document is based on RFC 4594, the security discussion in that document, which finds no new security issues, also applies to the treatment aggregates described here.
sections.plainLanguage: The document finds no new security problems. Grouping service classes only changes how the network treats traffic it was already allowed to treat, so it grants nothing new.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH OF THE FOUR AGGREGATES IS FOR

items.title: Network Control
items.text: Traffic the network needs to survive a flood. Low chance of loss, deep target queue depth.

items.title: Real-Time
items.text: Telephony, signalling, conferencing, interactive and broadcast traffic. Admitted and policed per class at the edge.

items.title: Assured Elastic
items.text: Traffic with a committed rate. Keeps its AF and class selector marks, so committed and excess traffic stay distinguishable.

items.title: Elastic
items.text: Standard and low-priority data. No service level promise, only queue management and congestion marking.
